message:
Love this reading, Mike.  It may seem an odd move, but I want to draw your attention to Elliot Eisner's Type III learning objectives.  In the context of Skinnerian Behavioral Objectives and Bloom's Cognitive Objectives, Eisner argues that in expressive learning (such as art and writing), one cannot specify the outcomes in advance.  Rather, one can specify a set of conditions likely to produce good outcomes, some of which may be better than the teacher/curriculum planner anticipated.

This takes us beyond the limitations of structuralism, with its assumption that all components (say of the writing process) could be specified and addressed.  It is humanistic, though not especially romantic, in my view.

I have consciously organized my FYC course along these lines, claiming to my students that the work they do will prepare them for academic, professional and civic literacy demands, arguing against a self (expressionist) and public (structuralist) dichotomy, and rather have them produce texts along this continuum:  self, other, group.  In this context, the self never goes away, but it can be submerged or foregrounded according to purpose and audience.  Kinda like blog-writing.  : )
